steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Official statistics: recorded by the police and published by the Home Office. They show that working-class people, men, young people and some ethnic minorities are over-represented. However, official statistics have major limitations: the 'dark figure of crime' (unreported and unrecorded crime) means they significantly underestimate true crime rates.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: The dark figure of crime: only about 40% of crime is reported to the police. Reasons: too trivial, police can't do anything, fear of retaliation, embarrassment. Of reported crime, only about 30% is recorded. The real crime rate is much higher than official statistics suggest.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Self-report studies: anonymous surveys asking people what crimes they have committed. Show that middle-class people commit more crime than official statistics suggest, especially white-collar crime. These studies challenge the class bias in official statistics.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Gender and crime: men commit about 80% of recorded crime. Heidensohn: women are controlled at home, in public, and at work. Chesney-Lind: women's crime is often a response to abuse. The gender gap is narrowing (female crime rates are rising).

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Explain why official statistics may not provide an accurate picture of crime. | Evaluate explanations for why men commit more crime than women. | Assess whether ethnic differences in crime statistics reflect real differences in criminality.
